html:
The basal ganglia, as described across these four subsections, constitute a structured, multi-objective policy optimizer embedded within–and reciprocally coupled to–a cortical generative model that it does not itself construct. The architecture can be summarized along four interlocking axes: what is optimized, what signal drives the optimization, how that signal writes into the circuit, and what behavioral and cognitive competences emerge from the resulting learning dynamics.

What is optimized. The BG do not minimize a single scalar loss. They minimize a family of coupled objectives distributed across parallel cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, each parameterized by a territory-specific discount factor, a territory-specific state representation inherited from upstream cortex, and a territory-specific behavioral domain. Ventral striatal loops optimize long-horizon motivational valuation; dorsomedial loops optimize intermediate-horizon, flexible action-outcome contingencies; dorsolateral loops optimize short-horizon sensorimotor execution and sequence consolidation; and posterior/tail loops stabilize sensory-action mappings through value-free repetition signals. Within each territory, the objective is not raw reward but constrained subjective utility: the reward term is nonlinearly transformed by the organism’s risk attitude, temporal discounting, effort costs, physiological need, and subjective probability weighting–a utility already expressed in the organism’s internal currency before it enters the TD computation. Layered atop this transformed reward are regularizers–energetic cost balanced through opponent D1/D2 pathway integration, policy complexity penalized in the dopaminergic signal itself, homeostatic and allostatic need defining the objective’s operating point, and STN-mediated commitment thresholds imposing sparse, non-impulsive selection under conflict. The cortical loss and the BG loss are complementary rather than competing: cortex minimizes precision-weighted prediction error to build and refine a high-dimensional generative world model (epistemic adequacy), while the BG minimize evaluative error to select, time, energize, and automatize policies over the state space that model provides (pragmatic adequacy). Together they form a coupled optimizer pair in which world-model learning and policy learning are analytically separable but biologically inseparable — each training under conditions partly created by the other, linked through the recurrent loop of action, sampling, and cortical updating.

What signal drives the optimization. The teaching signal is phasic dopamine, but "phasic dopamine" is itself a structured, heterogeneous population code rather than a single scalar broadcast. At the most classical level, midbrain dopamine neurons compute a temporal-difference reward prediction error through a distributed, multi-layered subtraction: VTA GABA interneurons supply a local subtractive expectation signal; the LHb–RMTg disynaptic pathway conveys worse-than-expected outcome information; and excitatory afferents from PPTg, lateral hypothalamus, and ventral pallidum supply the outcome and predicted-value terms–with most monosynaptic inputs already carrying mixed, partially pre-computed error signals rather than clean modular components. This classical RPE is then unfolded along two axes. Along the magnitude axis, individual dopamine neurons display stable heterogeneity in their asymmetric scaling of positive versus negative errors, implementing a distributional code in which different channels converge to different quantiles of the return distribution; downstream, D1 and D2 SPNs complete this code by preferentially encoding the optimistic and pessimistic tails, respectively, yielding an opponent distributional representation that supports risk-sensitive policy optimization. Along the temporal axis, dopamine transients follow a ventral-to-dorsolateral gradient of reward time horizons across striatal territories, and individual dopamine neurons carry stable, cell-intrinsic discount factors that are correlated across tasks, so that the population encodes something approaching the full joint distribution of future reward over both magnitude and time.

Beyond reward value, dopamine has been shown to carry prediction errors over sensory identity, associative transitions between value-neutral states, action execution relative to an action prior, and ongoing movement trajectories–each implemented by anatomically distinguishable subpopulations projecting to distinct striatal targets. The unifying principle is not a shared objective but a shared computational motif: each channel computes a prediction error relative to some expected state of the world, broadcasts it via dopaminergic release, and uses it to update the synaptic weights of the circuits that generated the prediction. Dopamine is therefore best understood not as a neurotransmitter synonymous with reward, but as a general-purpose credit assignment signal–one whose reward-value channel is the best-characterized instance of a much larger family of teaching signals. Yet this generality is not unconstrained. Corticostriatal and mesocortical dopaminergic innervation are anatomically biased toward cortical areas processing policy-relevant variables, and the inputs that set the dopaminergic prediction baseline are heavily weighted toward hypothalamic and interoceptive channels, ensuring that the system–however broad its learning scope–remains anchored to the organism’s biological preference distribution. Once the dopaminergic signal reaches the striatum, it enters a cholinergic field that finalizes its local instructional form: cholinergic pauses gate when dopamine becomes plasticity-relevant, the phase relationship between acetylcholine and dopamine demixes multiplexed dopamine into a plasticity-promoting teaching mode versus a transient vigor/performance mode, and in some territories cholinergic dynamics carry their own error-like signals that are especially important for extinction, reversal, and negative updating.

How the signal writes into the circuit. The canonical site of BG learning is the corticostriatal glutamatergic synapse onto spiny projection neurons, where the cortical state representation (the "what") meets the dopaminergic teaching signal (the "how good") at the subcellular level of a single dendritic spine. Learning is governed by a three-factor rule: Hebbian (and/or variants of Hebbian) learning establishes a molecularly defined eligibility trace–a silent synaptic tag lasting approximately 1–2 seconds, implemented through calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclase gated by high phosphodiesterase activity in SPN dendrites–that is converted into lasting potentiation or depression only when phasic dopamine arrives within the eligibility window. The sign of plasticity is determined by opponent pathway-specific decoding: D1 receptor activation drives PKA-dependent potentiation in direct-pathway SPNs, while D2 receptor relief and A2A-dependent signaling drive potentiation in indirect-pathway SPNs, such that a dopamine burst simultaneously reinforces the chosen action (via dSPNs) and weakens the representation of suppressing that action (via iSPNs), while a dopamine dip does the reverse. This opponent rule requires–and recent evidence confirms–that functionally opponent dSPNs and iSPNs are coactive during action selection, resolving a long-standing computational inconsistency about which synapses receive credit for negative outcomes. The eligibility window at the synapse is extended across longer delays by two complementary mechanisms: temporal-difference chaining, in which backward propagation of value through learned state sequences brings the relevant prediction error within the synaptic eligibility window at each step; and sustained prefrontal-to-striatal activity, which maintains the corticostriatal input pattern across the delay period until the teaching signal arrives. Cholinergic pauses add a further gating layer, restricting plasticity to epochs when CIN firing is suppressed, dopamine is phasic, and the SPN is depolarized–a triple-coincidence requirement that prevents irrelevant dopaminergic events from corrupting stored action values.

The SPN’s intrinsic electrophysiology provides the foundational gate: deeply hyperpolarized down states, enforced by Kir2 channels, render the neuron unresponsive to sparse or uncorrelated input; only convergent, synchronized cortical drive can promote the SPN into the depolarized up state–or, at finer resolution, trigger NMDA-dependent dendritic plateau potentials on individual branches–from which plasticity-relevant calcium dynamics and spiking become possible. These molecular primitives are, however, not uniformly parameterized across the striatum. DMS expresses symmetric anti-Hebbian STDP favoring flexible rewriting; DLS expresses asymmetric anti-Hebbian STDP favoring durable stabilization; NAc core shows bidirectional plasticity from a single induction protocol with distinct calcium-signaling mechanisms; and striosomal versus matrix compartments experience opposite dopaminergic modulation of up-state dynamics. The effective learning rule at each territory is thus matched to the computational demands of that territory’s position in the cortico-basal ganglia hierarchy: rapid revision where flexibility is needed, progressive consolidation where stability is needed, and compartment-specific evaluation-versus-execution separation where the critic must be distinguished from the actor.

What emerges. From these interacting components–territory-specific losses, structured heterogeneous error signals, and regionally parameterized plasticity rules–emerge the behavioral and cognitive competences that define the BG’s contribution to adaptive behavior. The exploration-exploitation tradeoff is not solved by a single mechanism but by a layered portfolio: opponent D1/D2 distributional coding provides uncertainty estimates that support directed exploration; transient dopaminergic novelty signals solve the cold-start problem for unfamiliar options; the DMS indirect pathway monitors policy reliability and triggers exploratory switching when accumulated negative evidence exceeds a threshold; and hypothalamic-to-tail-of-striatum circuitry globally modulates exploration scope as a function of homeostatic need–each mechanism operating concurrently, with their relative influence shifting as a function of task phase, environmental volatility, and internal state. Skill acquisition unfolds as a progressive redistribution of influence across the territory-specific loss landscape: from ventral striatal value scaffolding and dorsomedial flexible contingency learning during early goal-directed acquisition, through competitive rebalancing toward dorsolateral consolidation under positively biased dopamine and asymmetric plasticity, to crystallized chunking in which task-bracketing boundary signals, fine-grained kinematic control, and cortical disengagement mark the endpoint of policy compilation. This is not a serial handoff but a continuously negotiated competition between territories, with lateral orbitofrontal cortex regulating the balance and DMS actively restraining premature automatization. The same optimization architecture extends without modification to the cognitive domain: through associative and limbic cortico-basal ganglia loops, the BG gate working-memory updating, attentional allocation, task-set selection, hierarchical rule use, and–at the most abstract level–strategy deployment and meta-learning, with opponent D1/D2 plasticity training these cognitive gating policies just as it trains motor ones. The developmental trajectory of the system mirrors its hierarchical adult architecture, booting from the bottom up: homeostatic anchoring first, mesolimbic reward learning second, sensorimotor habit learning third, associative goal-directed policy learning fourth, and full cognitive gating last–each layer becoming available only as the required cortical, dopaminergic, and corticostriatal infrastructure comes online, and the earliest-learned value functions occupying a privileged position that structurally constrains all subsequent learning.

The deepest lesson of this chapter, then, is that the basal ganglia are not a reward tracker, not a habit machine, and not a motor controller–though they contribute to all three. They are the brain’s general-purpose policy optimizer: a constrained, biologically grounded, developmentally bootstrapped engine of credit assignment that learns, through a structured population of dopaminergic prediction errors operating on opponent corticostriatal plasticity, which cortical computations to gate, energize, suppress, or automatize–whether those computations produce a movement, a memory update, or a thought. What makes the system powerful is not any single mechanism but their conjunction: distributional coding gives it access to uncertainty; multi-timescale discounting gives it access to temporal structure; opponent pathway plasticity gives it asymmetric channels for reinforcement and suppression; territory-specific parameterization gives it the capacity to learn qualitatively different kinds of policies in parallel; cholinergic gating gives it temporal precision in credit assignment; and homeostatic grounding gives it an objective function anchored to biological viability rather than arbitrary reward maximization. What makes the system constrained is equally important: its teaching signal is anatomically restricted to policy-relevant cortical representations, its prediction baseline is weighted by interoceptive state, its eligibility windows are molecularly bounded, and its developmental ordering ensures that abstract cognitive policies are always built atop–and remain tethered to–the homeostatic value functions that first activated the dopaminergic teaching machinery. The result is a policy optimizer that is genuinely general in scope but not free to learn anything: a flexible optimization method operating within hard boundaries set by evolution, development, and anatomy, whose collective effect is to ensure that however much the basal ganglia learn about sensory identity, associative structure, action priors, cognitive strategies, and abstract goals, they remain a tool for keeping the organism within its preference distribution–a distribution that is itself inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first powered the system’s learning.
